concept.name: Symmetrical triangle
concept.definition: A classical consolidation pattern in which at least two lower highs and two higher lows produce converging trend lines, forming a contracting trading range. It is directionally neutral until the breakout: most often it resolves as a continuation of the prevailing trend, but a meaningful minority mark reversals. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Buyers and sellers reach into each other with shrinking swings, like a coiling spring; the stored-up indecision is released in whichever direction price finally escapes the converging lines.
concept.mechanics: Require a minimum of four turning points (two lower highs, two higher lows), ideally six; volume should diminish as the range contracts. The most reliable breakouts occur roughly halfway to three-quarters of the distance from base to apex, on a closing basis, ideally with volume expansion and possibly a 3% price or 3-day time filter; the apex later acts as support/resistance. Targets are estimated by projecting the widest part of the triangle from the breakout or by drawing a parallel trend line.
concept.formula: Price target = B +/- (H - L), where B = breakout price and H - L = the widest vertical distance of the triangle (sign follows breakout direction).
concept.failure_modes: Breakouts very close to the apex tend to be weak and meaningless, and premature or false breakouts are common — Edwards and Magee estimated roughly 25% of symmetrical triangles mark reversals rather than continuations. Guessing the breakout direction in advance is the classic mistake.
concept.misconceptions: That the triangle predicts the breakout direction — by construction it is neutral, and only the actual break (preferably with volume) assigns direction. Also, a contraction shorter than about three weeks is conventionally classified as a pennant, not a triangle.
concept.example: After a year-long downtrend, a stock coils for five months between falling highs and rising lows, then breaks down through the lower line with accelerating volume; the 10.5-point height projects a decline toward $19 from the $29.50 break.
